newsitem.title: JAPAN: Minor Metals -- Cobalt seen firm on low Congo output.
newsitem.headline: Minor Metals -- Cobalt seen firm on low Congo output.

text.p: Cobalt prices are expected to resume their advance after pausing for breath, amid talk of falling production in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the former Zaire, traders said on Tuesday.
"Prices are going to rise a little further, probably to around $25 (per pound) for high-grades," said a trader at one of Japan's leading trading houses.
"There's no doubt that Gecamines' production is going to fall this year, although the situation seems to be improving," he said.

Sources in Tokyo close to Gecamines, the state cobalt producer in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, said the country was reeling from the after-effects of a seven-month civil war, with its output in 1997 set to sink to well below 4,000 tonnes.
One source said: "We heard Gecamines has revised downwards its production forecast for this year to about 3,100 tonnes from an earlier forecast of 3,500 tonnes."

High-grade cobalt was quoted at $22.00-23.50 per pound and low-grade metal at $19.00-20.50. Few deals were struck as the Northern Hemisphere has entered the summer period of weak demand, traders said.

They added that they would also carefully watch a U.S. cobalt industry meeting on July 31, called by the Defense National Stockpile Center to discuss how to sell strategic stockpiles of the metal following legal battles with Minor Metals Inc.
Traders said prices for molybdenum oxide eased to around $4.50 per pound as many users have finished buying their requirements for the July-September quarter.
Talk that Molycorp of the U.S. will start delivering product to Japan over the next few months and high production levels in Chile weighed on the market, they added.

"Demand for both molybdenum and vanadium is fairly strong, but molybdenum prices are tending to ease due to ample supplies while vanadium prices remain firm due to tight physical supplies," one trader said.
Another trader agreed, adding: "Molybdenum will remain weak. Prices are likely to drop to $4.20-4.30."
In the magnesium market, Chinese offer prices were firm at $2,450-2,500 per tonne, as strong European demand continued to underpin the prices, traders said.

The first exports of metal from a new Isreali facility on the bank of the Dead Sea are unlikely to find many buyers in Japan, where there is strong competition from cheap Chinese metal and top-quality Western maganesium, traders said.
Chinese antimony was indicated at $1,900/1,975 per tonne basis C&F Rotterdam, as demand in Europe and the United States has slackened, traders said.
Chinese antimony production was not thought to have been affected by recent heavy rains in southern regions of the country, a European trader in Hong Kong said.
"There might be some transportation problems but at the moment stocks are still higher than demand so there are no supply hitches," he said.
The bismuth market remained well-balanced, traders said, with Chinese product indicated at $3.70/3.80 per lb for small lots up to five tonnes and $3.60/3.65 for bigger lots.
Peak demand coincides with the September to December hunting season in North America and Western Europe, where bismuth is replacing lead in cartridges.
"This (cartridges) now accounts for 15 to 20 percent of world consumption so we should start to see a slight increase around that time," one trader said.
Chinese supplies were ample. The European source said Chinese producers and traders could be relied upon to have at least 100 tonnes at any time.
"In general, bismuth in China will always be the last to follow the market down in prices," another trader said.
Indium demand remained healthy with prices, indicated in London late last week at $2.40/2.70 per kg of indium ingot, considered to have bottomed out.
